Chapter 5: What Can Be Shown but Not Said—The Unsayable in Ethics, Aesthetics, and the Mystical
So, as we start to really understand the logical structure of language, something interesting comes up. What about those parts of life that feel deeply meaningful... but somehow slip through our ability to pin down with words? Think about ethics, beauty, or those moments that feel almost mystical. We know they're important, but they just don't fit into neat statements or logical facts.
Picture this: you're listening to a piece of music that moves you, or you're standing in awe as the sun sets, painted across the sky. Or maybe you feel certain that something is right—or wrong—even though you can't quite explain why. These experiences aren't just facts about the world. They're something more, something that goes beyond what language can state outright.
This is where the difference between what can be said, and what can only be shown, really matters. The rules of logic, and the very structure of language itself, can be demonstrated by watching language in action—but you can't just state them flat out. In the same way, the deepest values and experiences? They can be lived, and they can be felt, but not fully described with words.
Here are a few key ideas to keep in mind.
Some parts of life—like ethics, beauty, and the mystical—can't be captured in straightforward, factual language. They're still incredibly meaningful, but their meaning lives outside what we can say. In fact, sometimes the most important things are exactly those that can't be spoken, only shown through how we experience them.
And here's something to pay attention to: recognizing the limits of language is a kind of wisdom in itself.
But don't think this makes values or beauty any less real. If anything, it highlights just how unique—and essential—they are to being human. They're not facts to be listed, but reminders that language, for all its power, has its boundaries. Beyond those boundaries lies a kind of meaning you can only hint at, live out, or show by example.
So, as we journey through the logical side of language, we don't end up with a tidy final answer. Instead, we come face to face with the limits of what can be said. The world of facts and logic is huge, no doubt—but it's not the whole story. Some things, we simply have to pass over in silence. And that's not because they aren't important... it's because they're so important, words just can't reach them.
